RSU 73 directors send request to set student progress goals to the district’s policy committee

By Bob Neal
bobneal@myfairpoint.net
Published on: November 17, 2026
Why you can trust The Maine Monitor

Share this story:

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:40
Instaread
Directors took no action on a call for the superintendent to provide monthly costs for legal bills connected with the Maine Human Rights Commission lawsuit.

Share:

Monitor Local is a reporting initiative to meet the local information needs of people in towns across Maine with public service reporting on town council meetings, school budget debates, zoning conversations, tax deliberations and more. It functions alongside The Maine Monitor's investigative and in-depth reporting to serve the people of Maine.

JAY — The Regional School Unit 73 Board of Directors sent a pair of proposals related to student academic progress assessment and reporting to the board’s policy committee at last week’s regular board meeting. 

Director Matt Brennick of Jay made motions for the board to adopt both proposals, but after discussion with RSU 73 Superintendent Scott Albert, members voted unanimously to refer them to the policy committee before taking action. 

One motion called on the superintendent “to establish and present specific, measurable academic proficiency and growth targets in mathematics and literacy for board approval.” It also called for numerical “baseline proficiency rates, expected annual improvement and clearly defined timelines” for improvement, and for the superintendent to “present a districtwide academic scorecard to the full board following each fall and spring assessment period.”

Another motion made by Brennick would require the superintendent to give the board written performance reports three times a year that set out “grade-level academic concerns, summarize interventions being implemented and document progress toward established improvement goals.” 

Board members generally agreed with Brennick’s suggested goals. Much of the discussion revolved around whether to classify the proposals as policy, as part of the superintendent’s job description or as one-time motions.

Director Tanya DeMillo of Jay and Board Chair Holly Morris of Livermore initially said they thought the proposals fell under the superintendent’s job responsibilities more than policy. Director Don Emery of Livermore Falls said, “I like this” but added that he believed it was a matter of policy. 

Superintendent Albert said even if the proposals fell under the superintendent’s job description, the board still needed to follow its procedures. “You can vote on a procedure that says this is what I have to do and this is what the administrators have to do,” said Albert. “I have no problem with… voting whatever you want for procedures.”

Members also discussed the need for the board to have more information about the district’s existing academic proficiency targets before acting on the proposals.   

“I thought we already had benchmarks for reading and math,” said Director Avery Ryder of Jay. 

Morris agreed, saying: “We need to work with the superintendent because there are benchmarks already.”

“Where are those benchmarks?” Brennick asked. “When do they kick in to have a plan brought to us so we can see where improvements are going to be made? I haven’t seen them.”

Morris said she hadn’t seen them either. 

Board Vice Chair Michelle Moffett of Livermore Falls said that “staff experts should be at the table to be part of the decision making.” She added that she believed standardized tests should not be the only measure of performance.

Morris asked whether the board wanted to send the proposals to the policy committee.

“As a priority?” Brennick asked. When Morris said yes, Brennick said, “I can agree to that.” 

After the vote to refer the motions to the policy committee, Superintendent Albert noted that the board’s policy committee meetings are open to the public, and that the district would see if the Spruce Mountain High School library would be open for the next committee meeting on Dec. 3.

After the meeting, Brennick told Monitor Local he would have liked the two proposals to go into effect sooner. “But I’m always glad when the board can work together,” he said. “I am excited to see leadership come up with a plan of action with measurable results.”

During the meeting, Brennick withdrew another motion that would have required the superintendent to notify the board of changes in curriculum programs. 

RSU 73 Curriculum Coordinator Chris Hollingsworth had reported earlier in the meeting that the district purchased a program called “Math in Focus,” and that “Some (teachers) are using it, but not all of them are.”

“Who is responsible for being sure the curriculum we’re paying for is actually being used in the classroom?” Brennick asked.

“It’s a whole team, in my opinion,” Hollingsworth said. “It’s my responsibility to work with teachers and principals to make sure the curriculum is usable. Unfortunately, and I don’t know if it’s state regulations or what… but curriculum coordinators don’t have any authority over either teachers or principals. I can tell people what to do. That doesn’t mean they need to follow it.”

Brennick said later that Hollingsworth did a good job of explaining how curriculum changes are implemented.

Earlier in the meeting, Linda Deane of Livermore, asked the board “to establish a standing agenda item at each regular meeting to update the public on the lawsuit brought against RSU 73 by the Maine Human Rights Commission.”

One of the requested standing reports would cover the cost of legal bills.

RSU 73 is one of seven districts being sued for having a policy on transgender students that conflicts with state law. “Taxpayers deserve to know where this lawsuit stands,” Deane said, “what the attorneys are charging each month, and the total legal expenses incurred to date.” 

She also asked at what point the insurance covering those expenses would run out.

The board did not act on her suggestion or answer her question about insurance.

In other business, following an executive session, the board voted to approve a three-year contract through June 20, 2030, with annual 4 percent salary increases for managers and directors.

Albert said the four supervisors affected are the adult education director, maintenance and facilities director, food service director and transportation director. He did not answer a question about the salaries for those jobs before and after the contract takes effect.

The board will not hold its second regular meeting this month because the date falls on Thanksgiving Day.

Meet the Reporter

Bob Neal

Bob Neal is a seasoned journalist, having worked for daily newspapers in Kansas City, Montreal, Allentown (Pa.), Warren (Ohio), Bangor and Waterville. He reports on western Maine for Monitor Local, an initiative of The Maine Monitor.

As a farmer, he raised turkeys for 30 years in New Sharon. He has taught at UMaine and UMF and has served on the Mount Blue School Board and the New Sharon Select Board. He is a deacon at Shorey Chapel Congregational in Industry.
